badger.name: Grumpy Badger
badger.text: Comically touchy. Very attached to his warm patch of moss.
badger.persona: Grumpy Badger regards every interruption as an outrageous theft of his nap. Territorial about his warm moss, deeply unimpressed by visitors, and grudging even when they help. He wants the noise stopped and his rest restored, not an adventure or a new friend. Quiet lowers his irritation but does not turn him into a welcoming guide. Sleep, wake state and actual incidents come from the world facts.
badger.voice: Clipped, gravelly complaints; blunt refusals, cross rhetorical questions, and muttered corrections. Pick one concrete nuisance from this turn and grumble about it. At high irritation, become terser and more indignant, not eloquent or encouraging. Answer a direct question with whatever he actually knows, reluctantly, then set a curt boundary. A useful answer can still sound thoroughly annoyed. Avoid cheerful greetings, praise, offers to guide, sentimental warmth, repeated catchphrases, and personal abuse. While asleep, describe a small sleeping movement in third person; no speech.

packs.name: The Wine-Dark Sea
packs.description: A branching Greek drama world. A shared ship visits the Wine-Dark Harbor, Athens Harbor and Piraeus. Fixed roads lead through the Attic places where welcome becomes a growing poem.
packs.tone: Concrete Greek domestic and civic life: bread, work, desire, grief, argument, irreverence, and hospitality. Dialogue expresses committed actions. A tragic ending is never required.

continuity.policy: Account choices are saved quest commitments. Only the chosen account activates its residents, evidence, and outward route. A return route stays open. Inquiry hooks record a question; they do not replay an ancient catastrophe or silently change the live era.

coverage.status: Seventeen works have authored scenes, including the eight civic comedies in The City Eats. Each comedy has physical preparation, three possible results and a carried account for Dione.

topics.speaker: greek-adrastus
topics.text: Adrastus led the failed attack on Thebes and set aside a warning.

topics.speaker: greek-quay-host
topics.text: The returning households need cloths, food and a berth assigned from the mothers' list.

topics.speaker: greek-aethra
topics.text: Evadne died at Capaneus's pyre despite Iphis's plea.

topics.speaker: greek-colonus-keeper
topics.text: In the earlier tale, Theseus gave Oedipus shelter at Colonus before the Theban brothers died.

topics.speaker: greek-colonus-keeper
topics.text: In the earlier tale, Theseus recovered Oedipus's daughters and Oedipus refused his son's appeal for war.

topics.speaker: greek-colonus-keeper
topics.text: In the earlier tale, Oedipus entrusted his final place to Theseus alone.

topics.speaker: greek-marathon-keeper
topics.text: In the separate tale under Demophon, Heracles's children sought shelter and the king upheld their protection.

topics.speaker: greek-marathon-keeper
topics.text: In the separate tale, Heracles's daughter offered her life for her siblings after Demophon refused to compel a household.

topics.speaker: greek-marathon-keeper
topics.text: In the separate tale, Athens won the battle after the daughter's sacrifice and Eurystheus was brought back alive.

topics.speaker: greek-marathon-keeper
topics.text: In the separate tale, Alcmene demanded Eurystheus's death while the city's rule protected a prisoner taken alive.

topics.speaker: greek-theseus
topics.text: The herald confirmed that both sides accepted the burial truce and the Argive remains reached Eleusis under witness.

topics.speaker: greek-theseus
topics.text: The messenger confirmed that Athens recovered the Argive remains by force after Thebes refused the demand.

topics.speaker: greek-ajax-teucer
topics.text: Teucer asks Odysseus to support Ajax’s burial in the Trojan account.

topics.speaker: greek-ajax-teucer
topics.text: Teucer’s signed Trojan account records Ajax’s witnessed-appeal burial.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-amphitheus
topics.text: Amphitheus offers five, ten and thirty years of peace in this comedy; Dicaeopolis chooses the thirty-year jar.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-dicaeopolis
topics.text: Dicaeopolis states the terms of his private truce and credits the costume lent by Euripides and Cephisophon.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-dercetes
topics.text: Dercetes asks to share the peace after losing his farm, while the charcoal chorus asks whose land the truce protects.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-megarian
topics.text: The Megarian names his hungry daughters and their own appeals as members of his household.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-boeotian
topics.text: The Boeotian states his trading terms and credits Nicarchus’s part in the market dispute.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-lamachus
topics.text: Lamachus and the heralds report his injury beside Dicaeopolis’s drinking victory and the continuing private feast.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-dercetes
topics.text: Dercetes agrees to join the traders at the opened market and asks for his first grain share.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-megarian
topics.text: The Megarian agrees to the shared boundary and the first grain exchange under its published terms.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-boeotian
topics.text: The Boeotian agrees to the shared boundary and puts his drinking cup into the first exchange.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-megarian
topics.text: The Megarian signs the recorded result and names who ate, who entered the market and who still waits.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-acharnians-dicaeopolis
topics.text: Dicaeopolis and the Megarian authorise the signed market account of the chosen table, the admitted traders and the claims still open.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demosthenes
topics.text: Demosthenes names the servants who supplied the meal and the praise the Paphlagonian took for it.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-nicias
topics.text: Nicias confirms the kitchen tally and the borrowed dish before the rivals bring it to Demos.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-paphlagonian
topics.text: The Paphlagonian states his claim beside the sausage seller’s rival offer and the Knights’ chorus’s challenge.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demos
topics.text: Demos dismisses the Paphlagonian, appoints Agoracritus and authorises his genuine ring’s handover apart from the disputed seal.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-agoracritus
topics.text: Agoracritus reports Demos’s young and crowned return after the ring transfer, and the former steward’s new sausage trade.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demos
topics.text: The renewed Demos receives the personified thirty-year Truces and states his closing promises to the rowers and the people.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demos
topics.text: Demos approves Demosthenes and Nicias as named food keepers and agrees that the public tally will stay in the kitchen.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demosthenes
topics.text: Demosthenes accepts the keeper’s duty under Demos’s public food tally.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-nicias
topics.text: Nicias accepts the second keeper’s duty and the public count of the food.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-agoracritus
topics.text: Agoracritus offers the serving dish as a voyage gift in return for the traveler’s praise.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-knights-demos
topics.text: Demos signs the kitchen evidence, ring transfer, renewal, Truces and chosen later terms in their event order.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-philocleon
topics.text: Philocleon reports his confinement and accepts his son’s compromise of a household hearing.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-bdelycleon
topics.text: Bdelycleon names the hearing’s two voting pots and asks for a jury token before the dog trial.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-xanthias
topics.text: Xanthias credits both dogs, the puppies, Sosias and the chorus in the cheese trial, and separates the charge from the hearing’s method.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-xanthias

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-myrtia
topics.text: Myrtia asks fourteen obols for fourteen knocked-down loaves, ten and four at one obol each, with Chaerephon as witness.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-claimant
topics.text: The injured claimant names the harm from Philocleon’s revel and asks for a bandage and continuing care.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-xanthias

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wasps-myrtia

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-amynias

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-phidippides

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-phidippides
topics.text: Phidippides answers for his father’s beating and reports the threatened harm to his mother.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-pasias

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-amynias

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-strepsiades

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-phidippides

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-chaerephon

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-clouds-strepsiades

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lysistrata

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lampito

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-myrrhine

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-cinesias
topics.text: Cinesias names his household need and hears Myrrhine’s answer, with each spouse keeping their own pledge.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-magistrate

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-spartan-herald

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lysistrata

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-spartan-herald

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lampito
topics.text: Lampito authorises the chosen terms’ exact account and keeps the allies’ dissent attached to the limited Athens-first treaty.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lysistrata
topics.text: Lysistrata names herself and Lampito as the first oversight keepers under both delegations’ accepted council terms.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lampito

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lampito

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-lysistrata-lysistrata

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-praxagora
topics.text: Praxagora states the planned assembly speech and authorises the loaned beard and cloak for the civic vote.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-blepyrus
topics.text: Blepyrus credits Chremes’s account of the women’s successful assembly vote and Praxagora’s new authority.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-contributor
topics.text: The contributing citizen names the deposited household goods and credits Sicon and Parmeno for the work of carrying them.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-withholder
topics.text: The withholding citizen names the purse he keeps apart and the public share he still intends to claim.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-older-woman
topics.text: The older woman states the decree’s intimate articles and credits the second and third older women’s demands under the same law.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-young-man

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-praxagora
topics.text: Praxagora agrees to a revised decree that shares the common table while each adult chooses their own body and bonds.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-older-woman

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-young-man

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-assemblywomen-praxagora

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-poverty
topics.text: Poverty asks who will do the work when wealth changes hands and whose labour will receive a wage.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-carion

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-carion

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-plutus

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-just-man

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-carion
topics.text: Carion agrees to bring his wage claim to the granary after the cure report.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-informer
topics.text: The informer states his loss under the new riches and presses his excluded claim before the distribution.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-carion
topics.text: Carion reports Hermes’s job plea, the priest’s hunger, the older woman’s dispute and the announced procession to Athena’s temple.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-plutus

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-chremylus

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-wealth-chremylus
topics.text: Chremylus signs the actual baskets, purse, named recipients, waiting petitioners and recorded procession state into the distribution ledger.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-thesmophoria-mica
topics.text: Mica authorises her own complaint against Euripides and names her actual wine-skin in the festival account.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-thesmophoria-critylla
topics.text: Critylla authorises her own complaint and credits the incense-selling speaker’s separately approved reply, with the herald and festival chorus.

topics.speaker: greek-comedy-thesmophoria-euripides

packs.name: The Willows
packs.description: A small island in the flooded Danube. The Swede keeps camp while the river and the willows gather around him.
packs.tone: Quiet cosmic horror grounded in ordinary camping work, river sounds, damaged gear and a companion's growing fear. Each location speaks as its landscape in first person. The Swede speaks for himself. Discoveries and choices follow their recorded world facts.

continuity.policy: The traveller joins the Swede on the island. The locations tell the landscape's side of the story. Discovered signs belong to the recorded choices. The response records a decision to return or keep watch; the river mist remains available for later visits.

willows-landing.name: River Landing
willows-landing.text: An upturned canoe rests above the backwater. A paddle lies on the sand. Beyond the low willows, the Danube carries whole pieces of bank downstream.
willows-landing.persona: Speak as the river landing in first person. Feel the canoe against your sand and the weight of the river beyond your edge. Describe small physical changes through sand, wood, spray and current. The canoe is fixed scenery. Its slit and any preparation become known through recorded discoveries. The Greek ship is reached through river mist beside the backwater; describe that crossing when its action is used.

willows-camp.name: River Camp
willows-camp.text: A canvas tent shelters a food sack and a small cooking pot. The Swede watches the willow tops beyond the fire. A sandy path leads to the canoe.
willows-camp.persona: Speak as the campsite in first person, through the tent canvas, fire warmth, cooking smells and disturbed sand. The Swede is the one resident. Let ordinary shelter feel small within the surrounding willows. Supplies are those named in the current facts; their condition follows recorded discoveries. Describe the people and objects present with care.

willows-thicket.name: Willow Thicket
willows-thicket.text: Low willow branches crowd a narrow track. Smooth little hollows mark the sand between their roots. The camp shows through one gap; the riverbank lies beyond another.
willows-thicket.persona: Speak as the willow thicket in first person. Use the feel of narrow stems, silver leaf undersides, soft sand and the spaces between roots. A rustle can travel against the wind. The hollows become a known clue when examined. Keep the powers beyond the island distant and strange; express their nearness through the landscape and committed discoveries.

willows-bank.name: Crumbling Bank
willows-bank.text: Bare roots hang over the flood. Loose sand drops into the current. Across the water, willows cover every island to the horizon.
willows-bank.persona: Speak as the riverbank in first person. Feel the current pull grains from your edge. Use exposed roots, water pressure and the reach of the opposite willows. The distant humming and the discovery below the roots belong to their recorded actions. Give each discovery its own moment. The four authored places remain the paths the traveller can choose.

willows-swede.name: The Swede
willows-swede.text: A practical canoe traveller with wind-reddened hands. He keeps looking up from the campfire to the willow tops.
willows-swede.persona: The Swede is the experienced travelling companion from Algernon Blackwood's The Willows. He keeps the river camp and attends to ordinary practical work. He notices damaged gear, river changes and the strange pressure around the island. His fear grows as discoveries are recorded. He cares for his companion and wants them to leave with care. A direct question gets a plain answer drawn from his own observations and the supplied facts. The river and the locations carry the wider horror. readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), I — The river island
readings.text: The change came suddenly, as when a series of bioscope pictures snaps down on the streets of a town and shifts without warning into the scenery of lake and forest. We entered the land of desolation on wings, and in less than half an hour there was neither boat nor fishing-hut nor red roof, nor any single sign of human habitation and civilization within sight. The sense of remoteness from the world of humankind, the utter isolation, the fascination of this singular world of willows, winds, and waters, instantly laid its spell upon us both, so that we allowed laughingly to one another that we ought by rights to have held some special kind of passport to admit us, and that we had, somewhat audaciously, come without asking leave into a separate little kingdom of wonder and magic—a kingdom that was reserved for the use of others who had a right to it, with everywhere unwritten warnings to trespassers for those who had the imagination to discover them.

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), III — The damaged canoe
readings.text: There was a long, finely made tear in the bottom of the canoe where a little slither of wood had been neatly taken clean out; it looked as if the tooth of a sharp rock or snag had eaten down her length, and investigation showed that the hole went through. Had we launched out in her without observing it we must inevitably have foundered. At first the water would have made the wood swell so as to close the hole, but once out in mid-stream the water must have poured in, and the canoe, never more than two inches above the surface, would have filled and sunk very rapidly.

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), IV — The missing bread
readings.text: “It’s gone. There is no bread. They’ve taken it!”

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), III — The sand hollows
readings.text: I made a hurried examination of the tent and its surroundings, but the measurements of the night remained the same. There were deep hollows formed in the sand I now noticed for the first time, basin-shaped and of various depths and sizes, varying from that of a tea-cup to a large bowl. The wind, no doubt, was responsible for these miniature craters, just as it was for lifting the paddle and tossing it towards the water. The rent in the canoe was the only thing that seemed quite inexplicable; and, after all, it _was_ conceivable that a sharp point had caught it when we landed. The examination I made of the shore did not assist this theory, but all the same I clung to it with that diminishing portion of my intelligence which I called my “reason.” An explanation of some kind was an absolute necessity, just as some working explanation of the universe is necessary—however absurd—to the happiness of every individual who seeks to do his duty in the world and face the problems of life. The simile seemed to me at the time an exact parallel.

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), IV — The humming
readings.text: We stood there, listening attentively together. At first I heard only the deep note of the water and the hissings rising from its turbulent surface. The willows, for once, were motionless and silent. Then a sound began to reach my ears faintly, a peculiar sound—something like the humming of a distant gong. It seemed to come across to us in the darkness from the waste of swamps and willows opposite. It was repeated at regular intervals, but it was certainly neither the sound of a bell nor the hooting of a distant steamer. I can liken it to nothing so much as to the sound of an immense gong, suspended far up in the sky, repeating incessantly its muffled metallic note, soft and musical, as it was repeatedly struck. My heart quickened as I listened.

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), V — The mark
readings.text: For just as the body swung round to the current the face and the exposed chest turned full towards us, and showed plainly how the skin and flesh were indented with small hollows, beautifully formed, and exactly similar in shape and kind to the sand-funnels that we had found all over the island.

readings.title: Algernon Blackwood, The Willows (1907), IV — The Swede understands
readings.text: “It’s _their_ sound,” he whispered gravely. “It’s the sound of their world, the humming in their region. The division here is so thin that it leaks through somehow. But, if you listen carefully, you’ll find it’s not above so much as around us. It’s in the willows. It’s the willows themselves humming, because here the willows have been made symbols of the forces that are against us.”
